events.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and blast radius across services around 2026-05-05 09:10Z. Specifically: (1) exact onset time of order-service p99 > 5s (when did it first cross threshold, was it gradual or a step change at a specific minute?); (2) whether other services depending on or co-located with ledger-db show simultaneous latency/error degradation; (3) ledger-db's own metrics — query latency, active connections, lock waits, statement timeout counts — and whether DB load spike precedes or follows the order-service latency; (4) any node/CPU/IO saturation on the DB host. Report actual onset timestamps for each affected signal so they can be correlated with changes.

Identify every change made across ALL services in the 2026-05-05 00:00Z-09:30Z window, not just order-service and not just ledger-db. List deployments, config changes (especially the DBA autovacuum change — exact parameters, target tables, applied time), feature-flag/infra changes, and any shared-component changes. Also map order-service's dependency chain to ledger-db and identify other services sharing ledger-db or its host. Note any past incidents matching 'statement timeouts + autovacuum' or 'p99 latency after DB config change' with their root causes.

Determine the mechanism of the ledger-db statement timeouts: are they caused by lock contention/blocking chains (who blocks whom, e.g. a long-running transaction, a heavy vacuum process competing for IO), by CPU/IO saturation, or by slow individual queries from a new query pattern? Break down the DB wait events and identify the top blocking/consuming sessions in the 09:00-10:59Z window, and whether a specific table or query shape dominates. Depends on task a's onset time and task b's config-change list to focus the window.

args.query: p99 latency after DB config change autovacuum scale factor

events.statement: In the 2026-05-05T00:00Z-09:30Z window exactly one deployment occurred across all services: portfolio-service v4.5.0 at 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z by k.shah ('Add realised P&L breakdown to holdings API'), status live, not rolled back, with changes ['new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at','no migration included']. No order-service deployment in the window.

Exactly one config change was recorded in the window: ledger-db 'autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor' changed from 0.2 to 0.1 at 2026-05-05T08:00:00Z by dba-team, described 'More aggressive autovacuum'. This is the only ledger-db config change through 10:59Z.

order-service depends on ledger-db (edge kind 'db') directly, plus pricing-engine and exchange-gateway (http) and kafka (queue-produce). ledger-db is a shared=true postgres owned by platform and is called directly by FOUR services: order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service.

order-service's other shared downstream components (besides ledger-db) are kafka (queue-produce, shared) directly, and via pricing-engine/market-data-service: redis-cache (cache, shared). api-gateway is the only upstream caller of order-service.

Historical precedent HIST-110 (2026-01-15) matches the current symptom set most closely: 'Slow orders from ledger-db IOPS throttling', services [order-service, ledger-db], symptoms [order latency, statement timeouts, slow queries]; root cause was cloud volume burst credits exhausted -> IOPS throttled (not autovacuum). HIST-111 (2025-05-22) shows ledger-db slow queries/high db cpu caused by a new report query without index (bad_deployment), involving settlement-service.

The two changes in-window are close in time to the reported onset (09:10Z): ledger-db autovacuum scale factor changed at 08:00Z (70 min before report) and portfolio-service deployed at 08:56Z (14 min before report). portfolio-service also shares ledger-db, so it is both a caller of the affected DB and a fresh deployment.

events.statement: order-service latency_p99_ms shows a step change: steady ~143-167ms from 08:00-08:52Z, then the 08:56Z bucket (4-min bucket starting 08:56) already averages 1514.78ms (max 5607.8) and the first fully-over-5s bucket is 09:00Z at avg 5223.1ms; it then stays ~5000-5500ms through 10:00Z. Not gradual.

First order-service ERROR (statement timeout on INSERT INTO orders) is at 09:00:42Z (orderId=15a39d3b); 142 such ERRORs total in 08:00-10:00Z, all pattern 'ledger-db: canceling statement due to statement timeout (INSERT INTO orders)'. The only earlier WARN is a single unrelated 'retrying idempotent request' at 08:05:59Z.
ledger-db slow_queries_per_min jumped in the same 08:56Z bucket: steady ~0.8-1.3/min from 08:00-08:52Z, then 08:56Z avg 70.42 (max 139.68) and 09:00Z avg 143.45, holding ~135-148/min thereafter.

ledger-db connections_active jumped in the same 08:56Z bucket from ~60-64 (08:00-08:52Z) to avg 127.45 (max 199.81) at 08:56Z and ~185-197 thereafter, while cpu_pct went from ~30% to 63.26% (max 96.36) at 08:56Z and ~95-96% from 09:00Z on. Both onset in the same bucket as the order-service and portfolio-service latency step.

portfolio-service latency_p99_ms shows the same step and is the worst hit: steady ~174-195ms through 08:52Z, then 08:56Z avg 3574.3 (max 7056.7) and 09:00Z avg 6966.25, holding ~6800-7200ms through 10:00Z — worse than order-service (~5200ms).

ledger-db slow-query logs (185 WARN matches, first 08:58:38Z) are ALL the same pattern issued by application_name=portfolio-service: 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2 ORDER BY executed_at -- Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)'. No slow query in the returned window is attributed to order-service; order-service only appears as the client whose INSERTs are cancelled.

events.answer: All signals show a step change in the 08:56Z–09:00Z 4-minute bucket on 2026-05-05, not a gradual ramp. ledger-db slow queries per minute jumped from ~1/min to ~143/min and active connections from ~62 to ~190 in the 08:56Z bucket, with CPU going from ~30% to ~96%; portfolio-service p99 went 182ms -> 6966ms and order-service p99 143ms -> 5223ms in the same first bucket. The DB-side load spike and the dependent-service latency degradation are simultaneous (same 08:56Z bucket), so a DB-side blow-up precedes or coincides with — it does not follow — the order-service latency. The slow queries are driven by portfolio-service (Seq Scan on trades, 48M rows), and order-service timeouts are a downstream consequence. I could not pin the onset to a single minute (4-min buckets are too coarse) and could not query node/CPU/IO host metrics or lock waits because the tool budget ran out.

events.statement: Ledger-db logs contain NO lock contention, no blocking-chain and no deadlock evidence in the incident window: a WARN search for 'lock' over 08:50-10:59Z returned 0 matches, and a search for 'deadlock' over 05:00-10:59Z returned 0 matches. The only WARN pattern in ledger-db is the portfolio-service slow query. This rules out lock-wait/blocking-chain as the timeout mechanism.

Autovacuum activity is NOT anomalous or IO-heavy: ledger-db INFO logs show the routine 'autovacuum: processed table public.audit_log' cycle continuing at the same cadence (~every 4-30 min) both before and after the 08:00Z config change, up to 08:52:26Z and 10:55:51Z. The only autovacuum-related config line is 'config change cfg-2903 applied: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor=0.1' at 08:00:20Z. No vacuum-on-trades, no vacuum blocking, no long-running vacuum entry appears. This argues against autovacuum heavy-vacuum IO competition as the mechanism.

A single query shape dominates the DB load: ALL 49 ledger-db slow-query WARNs in 08:58:38-09:15Z are the same pattern from application_name=portfolio-service — 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2 ORDER BY executed_at -- Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)', with durations repeatedly 5-8.8s (first 8690ms at 08:58:38Z). No slow query in the window is attributed to order-service.

The trades Seq Scan onset at the minute level: slow_queries_per_min is flat ~0.7-1.1/min through the 08:53Z bucket (avg 1.06), then jumps to avg 47.34 (max 139.17) in the 08:56Z bucket and ~137-146/min from 08:59Z on. This matches the 08:56Z portfolio-service v4.5.0 deployment, i.e. the slow-query flood starts with/just after the new query going live, not at the 08:00Z autovacuum change.

Disk-related saturation is absent: ledger-db disk_used_pct is essentially flat and slowly declining across 08:00-09:30Z (avg ~70.7-71.8%, min 69.62, max 72.48, mean 71.03), with no step at 08:56Z. Combined with the CPU step, this indicates the bottleneck is CPU/query execution, not disk fill or an IO volume event.

Interpretation: the statement timeouts are a CPU-contention/collateral effect, not lock waits — the new portfolio-service Seq Scan on the 48.2M-row trades table floods ledger-db with multi-second queries, saturating shared CPU, so order-service INSERTs into orders queue and exceed their statement timeout. The autovacuum scale-factor change at 08:00Z is temporally separated (55+ min) from the 08:56Z load step and shows no vacuum-related blocking in logs.

events.description: Could not retrieve ledger-db CPU per-minute zoom for 08:40-09:20Z: the cpu_pct query was blocked by the tool-call budget (budget_exhausted), so the CPU step is only evidenced via T1's 08:56Z-bucket figures (~30%->96%), not re-confirmed at minute resolution in this task.

ledger-db exposes no wait-event / pg_stat_activity / pg_locks metric set (available_metrics = connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min) and no lock/deadlock/blocking log lines exist. There is no per-session blocking-chain ('who blocks whom') telemetry available.
No ledger-db log line records the autovacuum change's target table beyond public.audit_log routine processing; and the dummy cpu_pct requery and IOPS-volume metrics were not available/budget-blocked.

events.answer: The ledger-db statement timeouts are NOT lock contention/blocking-chain and NOT a heavy vacuum competing for IO: there are zero lock/deadlock/vacuum-blocking wait events in ledger-db logs, and autovacuum continues its routine 'processed table public.audit_log' cycle unchanged before and after the change. The mechanism is CPU saturation driven by a new query shape — a highly repetitive Seq Scan on the 48.2M-row trades table from portfolio-service v4.5.0 — which pins DB CPU at ~95-96% and makes unrelated INSERTs from order-service hit statement timeout. Disk usage stays flat (~71%), so IO/disk-fill is not the driver; IOPS throttling (HIST-110) is not supported by any observed disk signal.

tasks.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and blast radius across services around 2026-05-05 09:10Z. Specifically: (1) exact onset time of order-service p99 > 5s (when did it first cross threshold, was it gradual or a step change at a specific minute?); (2) whether other services depending on or co-located with ledger-db show simultaneous latency/error degradation; (3) ledger-db's own metrics — query latency, active connections, lock waits, statement timeout counts — and whether DB load spike precedes or follows the order-service latency; (4) any node/CPU/IO saturation on the DB host. Report actual onset timestamps for each affected signal so they can be correlated with changes.
tasks.answer: All signals show a step change in the 08:56Z–09:00Z 4-minute bucket on 2026-05-05, not a gradual ramp. ledger-db slow queries per minute jumped from ~1/min to ~143/min and active connections from ~62 to ~190 in the 08:56Z bucket, with CPU going from ~30% to ~96%; portfolio-service p99 went 182ms -> 6966ms and order-service p99 143ms -> 5223ms in the same first bucket. The DB-side load spike and the dependent-service latency degradation are simultaneous (same 08:56Z bucket), so a DB-side blow-up precedes or coincides with — it does not follow — the order-service latency. The slow queries are driven by portfolio-service (Seq Scan on trades, 48M rows), and order-service timeouts are a downstream consequence. I could not pin the onset to a single minute (4-min buckets are too coarse) and could not query node/CPU/IO host metrics or lock waits because the tool budget ran out.

tasks.answer: Across ALL services in 2026-05-05 00:00Z-09:30Z there were exactly two changes: a ledger-db config change (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1, 2026-05-05T08:00:00Z, by dba-team, 'More aggressive autovacuum') and one deployment (portfolio-service v4.5.0, 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z, k.shah, new trades query, no migration, live/not rolled back). order-service itself had no deployment. order-service reaches ledger-db directly (kind=db) and ledger-db is a shared platform postgres also used directly by portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service; order-service's other shared components are kafka (direct) and redis-cache (via pricing-engine/market-data-service). Precedents: HIST-110 (order latency + statement timeouts on ledger-db) was IOPS burst-credit throttling, not autovacuum; HIST-111 was a new unindexed report query slowing ledger-db.

tasks.objective: Determine the mechanism of the ledger-db statement timeouts: are they caused by lock contention/blocking chains (who blocks whom, e.g. a long-running transaction, a heavy vacuum process competing for IO), by CPU/IO saturation, or by slow individual queries from a new query pattern? Break down the DB wait events and identify the top blocking/consuming sessions in the 09:00-10:59Z window, and whether a specific table or query shape dominates. Depends on task a's onset time and task b's config-change list to focus the window.
tasks.answer: The ledger-db statement timeouts are NOT lock contention/blocking-chain and NOT a heavy vacuum competing for IO: there are zero lock/deadlock/vacuum-blocking wait events in ledger-db logs, and autovacuum continues its routine 'processed table public.audit_log' cycle unchanged before and after the change. The mechanism is CPU saturation driven by a new query shape — a highly repetitive Seq Scan on the 48.2M-row trades table from portfolio-service v4.5.0 — which pins DB CPU at ~95-96% and makes unrelated INSERTs from order-service hit statement timeout. Disk usage stays flat (~71%), so IO/disk-fill is not the driver; IOPS throttling (HIST-110) is not supported by any observed disk signal.
